title: LiLCA (Litter Impacts in LCA) Plastic Footprint Guide
text:
Preface
Life cycle assessment (LCA) is a standardized tool (ISO 14040) used to evaluate the impacts of products or services over their life cycle, from production to end-of-life, by evaluating impacts on ecosystem quality, human health, and ecosystem services and resources.
Up until recently, LCA of plastic products (and others) did not consider the impacts of plastic pollution emitted during their life cycles. New life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) metrics have allowed plastic pollution to be included in LCA, marking a significant step that should be adopted, especially for specific sectors such as packaging or textiles. As these advances are not generally known to the broader LCA community, this guide aims to facilitate integration of these new approaches in LCA.

text:
Objective
The objective of this methodological guide is to provide LCA practitioners with a detailed understanding of how to assess potential impacts associated with plastic emissions. The guide provides step-by-step support for practitioners seeking to implement the relevant characterization factors (CFs) in their assessments, from the identification and preparation of relevant inventory flows to the calculation and interpretation of midpoint and damage results. At the time of writing the first edition of this guide, the available CFs covered in this guide are the ones assessing physical effects on biota from microplastic ingestion. Other CFs will be included in future revisions.
This guide includes steps to assess the amount of plastic emitted over the life cycle of products, and employs the CFs developed by MarILCA, which link the emissions of plastic to their potential impacts on ecosystem quality. These CFs were developed within the MarILCA framework. The MarILCA working group was created in 2018 with the support of the Life Cycle Initiative of UN Environment and the Forum for Sustainability through Life Cycle Innovation (FSLCI), with the objective of integrating potential environmental impacts of marine litter, especially plastic, into LCA results. This effort aims to provide a more comprehensive picture of potential environmental impacts and to support the identification of trade-offs associated with the use of plastic and other materials in product systems.
Because these CFs may not yet be readily available or fully operationalized in commonly used LCA software and LCI databases, practitioners may need to perform complementary calculations outside their usual modeling workflow. Depending on the software, database, and modeling approach used, this may concern the preparation of the LCI, the application of CFs during LCIA, or both.
Using this guide should therefore enable practitioners with different levels of experience to consistently integrate contributions from plastic emissions into their LCAs, either at midpoint or damage level, while making transparent the assumptions, data choices, and calculation steps required for implementation.
This guide follows the plastic footprint definition of Corella-Puertas et al. (2026). The plastic footprint is defined as (1) the mass of plastic litter entering the environment (with information on the polymer type, size, shape), and (2) its environmental impacts (quantified via impact assessment metrics). Here, the assessment focuses on the “plastic physical footprint”. A free online tool is available to facilitate the calculations outlined in this guide.

title: LiLCA (Litter Impacts in LCA) Plastic Footprint Guide
text:
Content
This guide comprises six main sections following this preface.

Section 1 presents the rationale underpinning the development of the CFs, retraces their methodological development within the MarILCA framework, and explains what aspects of environmental impact they are intended to characterize. It situates the work within its broader methodological context and outlines both achieved milestones and ongoing developments.
Section 2 provides guidance on when the impact of plastic pollution should be accounted for in LCA studies. It discusses the practical implications of the current disconnect between available CFs and the limited representation of plastic litter flows in LCI databases. It then introduces screening questions to help practitioners determine whether further assessment is relevant and feasible.
Section 3 provides detailed step-by-step guidance for integrating the CFs into LCAs, covering the LCI, LCIA, and interpretation phases. Particular attention is given to key practical challenges, including the identification and selection of relevant inventory flows, the consistent application of CFs during impact assessment, and the robust interpretation of results.
Section 4 presents the main data sources currently available to support the quantification of plastic emissions in LCA studies. It reviews recent initiatives, including the Plastic Leak Project and the Plastic Footprint Network, that have contributed to the development of emission factors for activities and sectors prone to plastic leakage. The section also summarizes the current coverage of available data, highlights remaining gaps across sectors and emission pathways, and directs practitioners to relevant sources of information for estimating plastic emission flows within the scope of their assessments.
Section 5 presents fully developed case studies from selected industrial sectors, illustrating how the methodology is applied step by step and supporting correct implementation of the CFs. It also lists the published studies that include plastic impacts (Section 5.3).
Finally, Section 6 addresses recurring questions, frequently encountered issues, and methodological uncertainties. Users are encouraged to consult this section when encountering practical or conceptual challenges during their assessments.

title: 1  Background
text:
1.1 Plastics: functional benefits and environmental concerns
Plastics have become deeply embedded in modern economies due to their versatility, low density, durability, barrier properties, and relatively low production costs. These properties make them useful across a wide range of applications, including packaging, healthcare, construction, transportation, and electronics. In some systems, plastics can contribute to material efficiency, product protection, reduced transport burdens, or longer service life. These benefits should be acknowledged, because the environmental relevance of plastic products depends on the function delivered and on the full life cycle considered.
At the same time, the scale of plastic production and use has resulted in growing plastic stocks within the technosphere and increasing waste flows requiring end-of-life management. Yet only a limited fraction of plastic waste is successfully recycled globally, commonly estimated at 9%. As a result, substantial quantities of plastic waste are landfilled, incinerated, mismanaged, or released to natural environments. In an LCA context, the key issue is therefore not only the generation of plastic waste, but the fraction of plastic flows that may leave the technosphere and become plastic emissions to environmental compartments generating potential impacts.
Global assessments provide an indication of both the scale and the sources of plastic leakage to the environment. OECD estimates suggest that around 22 Mt of plastics entered natural environments in 2019, reflecting the combined effects of high plastic consumption and insufficient waste management systems (Figure 1.1). Most of these emissions were macroplastics (MaP), representing approximately 19.4 Mt, primarily associated with inadequate waste collection and disposal practices. Additional contributions arose from littering and marine-based activities. Although smaller in quantity, microplastics (MiP), typically defined as particles ranging from 1 µm to 5 mm, represent a significant fraction of total leakage. They are mainly generated through dust, tire abrasion, wastewater sludge, and losses of industrial plastic pellets (OECD 2022), in addition to fragmentation (Figure 1.1).
Once released into terrestrial, freshwater, or marine ecosystems, plastics can generate significant ecological impacts. Larger plastic debris, termed macroplastics, can be ingested by fauna or cause entanglement, leading to injury, impaired mobility, reduced feeding capacity, or mortality in birds, mammals, fish, reptiles or other taxa (Beaumont et al. 2019). Beyond these visible impacts, fragmentation processes driven by UV radiation, mechanical abrasion, and biological activity progressively generate smaller particles. Microplastics and nanoplastics (<1 µm size particles) resulting from this fragmentation are referred to as secondary microplastics, whereas primary microplastics refer to those that are intentionally produced and integrated into products at small sizes.
As particle size decreases, the spectrum of potentially exposed organisms broadens. Micro- (MiP) and nanoplastics can be ingested by a wide range of species, including zooplankton, benthic invertebrates, and other organisms at the base of trophic networks. In aquatic environments, exposure may occur through feeding, filtration, or ventilation processes (Wright et al. 2013; Besseling et al. 2015). Experimental evidence also indicates that micro- and nanoplastics can affect photoautotrophic organisms, including through effects on growth, photosynthetic activity, and oxidative stress, although responses vary depending on particle size, shape, polymer type, concentration, and exposure conditions (Zhang et al. 2017; Bhattacharya et al. 2010; Sjollema et al. 2016). Because these organisms contribute to primary production, nutrient cycling, and trophic transfer, effects at lower trophic levels may propagate through food webs and affect ecosystem functioning (Galloway et al. 2017; De Sá et al. 2018).
Given the scale of plastic production, the persistence of materials in the environment, and the diversity of exposure pathways and affected taxa, these impacts must be systematically considered when evaluating the environmental performance of products and services. Integrating Ecosystem Quality indicators related to plastic and microplastic emissions in LCA is therefore essential to ensure a more comprehensive and ecologically meaningful sustainability assessment of plastics and their alternatives.

1.2 History of the plastic litter issue in LCA

1.2.1 Inventory data developments
The Plastic Leak Project (PLP) (Peano et al. 2020) was the first science-based initiative aiming at developing inventory models allowing the quantification of plastic emissions towards the environment from various processes and activities. Their Sectorial Guidance Generic data allowed for the quantification of MiP or MaP leakage associated with four main processes, namely pellet production (MiPs), tire abrasion during transport (MiPs), microfiber releases from textile washing (MiPs) and losses occurring at the end-of-life through waste mismanagement or littering (MaPs) (Peano et al. 2020).
Building on this initiative, the Plastic Footprint Network (PFN) was launched in 2023 with a broader scope. While the PLP focused primarily on inventory models for quantifying plastic emissions, the PFN seeks to connect plastic emissions inventories with impact assessment within a single cohesive framework. For the impact assessment step, the PFN relies on MarILCA and therefore mainly focuses its efforts on the development of the inventory step. In this regard, several PFN technical modules have been developed to address key sources of plastic leakage across the life cycle, including packaging, textiles and textile fibers, tires, fishing gear, agricultural plastics, and leakage associated with waste exports.
Other assessments provide overviews of global emissions without aiming to allocate or scale these emissions to specific product systems or activities (Cottom et al. 2024; Han et al. 2026). Such studies are useful for identifying major sources and pathways of plastic leakage on a global scale, but they do not provide the activity-based emission factors or modeling structure required for assessments at the product or service scale.


1.2.2 Impact assessment developments

1.2.2.1 Physical effects on biota (microplastics)
The following overview focuses on the development of CFs representing physical effects on biota within the MarILCA framework. MarILCA currently provides one of the most operational approaches in LCIA for quantifying potential impacts associated with primary or secondary MiP emissions to the environment.
The development of these CFs responded to an important gap in standard LCA practice. Before the launch of the MarILCA working group, plastic leakage from product systems, and the environmental consequences associated with such emissions, were not accounted for. Commonly used inventories did not include dedicated flows for identifying and quantifying plastic releases to environmental compartments, while LCIA methods did not provide CFs to characterize their potential impacts. This gap was explicitly highlighted by the Medellin Declaration on Marine Litter in Life Cycle Assessment and Management, which called for the integration of plastic litter issues into both inventory modeling and impact assessment (Sonnemann and Valdivia 2017). It was subsequently addressed through the creation of the MarILCA working group in 2018.
Within this context, the first milestone was the development of a structured methodological framework to assess the potential impacts of plastic litter emissions Figure 1.2. Woods et al. (2021) formalized this framework and established a clear research agenda, identifying the key modeling components required to derive CFs. With this conceptual foundation in place, subsequent work focused on progressively operationalizing the different building blocks needed to quantify physical effects on biota.






Figure 1.2: Project framework and projects



The operationalization of this framework began in 2022, when the first of these building blocks was published introducing a generic effect factor to account for physical effects on biota (Lavoie et al. 2022). The effect factor was built on experimental data, considering effects on growth, reproduction and/or survival of species. Building on this contribution, Corella-Puertas et al. (2022) proposed an initial set of simplified CFs to estimate potential impacts on Ecosystem Quality resulting from emissions of expanded polystyrene and tire and road wear particles in aquatic environments. At that stage, the fate model was deliberately simplified, considering only degradation and sedimentation processes and relying on uncertain slow-to-fast degradation rates. Further methodological refinements followed, extending the framework to additional polymers and particle shapes. These developments culminated in the first official release of CFs in Corella-Puertas et al. (2023), which presented revised fate and effect factors.
Building on the 2023 release, subsequent developments broadened the model scope and improved its robustness. Saadi et al. (2025) incorporated impacts occurring in sediments, which had previously been omitted. This refinement led to substantial increases in CF values, particularly for high-density polymers whose longer residence times in sediments, combined with slow degradation processes, amplify potential impacts (Saadi et al. 2025). Saadi and Boulay (2026) also introduced CFs for semi-synthetic and cellulosic-based natural fibers in the marine environment. In early 2026, Louvet et al. (2026) provided another significant update aligning the fate modeling approach with the USEtox consensus framework for toxicity and ecotoxicity impact categories (Rosenbaum et al. 2008; Fantke et al. 2021), by integrating the multimedia fate modeling work of Quik et al. (2024). At that stage, the revised model was applicable to spherical MiPs only but included freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems for the first time. Finally, in late 2026, a consolidated and comprehensive version of the CFs named PEBBLE (Physical Effects on Biota and Biodiversity of Litter in the Environment) was released, extending coverage to the three particle shapes identified in earlier stages of the research, namely spheres, fibers, and films, expanding the range of polymers and materials considered, providing short- and long-term CFs, and integrating better degradation and marine transport modeling (Saadi et al. 2026). The resulting CFs are aligned with the USEtox approach by providing a consistent fate, exposure, and effect framework to characterize impacts in LCIA.
These CFs aim to quantitatively represent the potential detrimental physical effects of MiP emissions to natural environments on biodiversity, expressed under the area of protection Ecosystem Quality. CFs are provided in different units depending on their alignment with specific LCIA methods (IMPACT World+, ReCiPe, and GLAM). Despite these advances, important uncertainties remain, particularly regarding fragmentation (for inventory data) and degradation dynamics, species sensitivity data, and the scaling of organism-level effects to biodiversity damage metrics.


1.2.2.2 Entanglement impacts from fishing gear (MaPs)
Spatially explicit CFs to quantify potential impacts on Ecosystem Quality from entanglement-prone MaP debris, particularly lost fishing gear, have recently been developed by Høiberg et al. (2024). These CFs are provided at the scale of exclusive economic zones (EEZs) and as country-level averages, representing a significant advancement in the spatial differentiation of MaP impacts. However, their methodological framework is not fully aligned with the modeling approach used in MarILCA for MiP emissions, which limits their direct integration within a unified impact assessment framework.
First, the fate modeling underlying Høiberg et al. (2024) does not explicitly quantify the residence time of debris across environmental compartments in a manner consistent with multimedia fate modeling approaches typically applied in LCIA. The period during which debris may remain available to entangle organisms must therefore be assessed separately, which can be particularly challenging for non-experts. As a result, temporal dynamics are not treated in a way that is directly comparable to MiP fate modeling in Corella-Puertas et al. (2023), Saadi et al. (2025), or Louvet et al. (2026), or even other impact categories (e.g., ecotoxicity). Second, the effect modeling does not rely on endpoints such as mortality, impaired reproduction, or reduced growth, which are more directly aligned with the consensus toxicity framework used in USEtox (Rosenbaum et al. 2008). Instead, the approach estimates the fraction of potentially affected species based on their susceptibility to interacting with entanglement-prone MaP debris. This may lead to conservative estimates of potential impact, since not all interactions necessarily translate into ecologically relevant damage at the population level.
Finally, the scope of the CFs developed by Høiberg et al. (2024) is restricted to debris with entanglement-prone geometries, such as fishing nets and lines. This limits their applicability to a specific subset of MaP items and makes it difficult to systematically link these CFs to the diverse range of product shapes encountered in product-level LCAs outside the fishing industry. Consequently, while these CFs represent a valuable step toward integrating MaP entanglement impacts into LCIA, further methodological harmonization would be required to ensure consistency with MiP impact pathways.
Despite these limitations, these CFs have been tested in combination with CFs for physical effects on biota from MiP emissions in a fishing industry case study. The results showed that MaP entanglement impacts can be highly relevant for Ecosystem Quality, particularly for anchoveta fishing in Peru, where they dominated the results under the assumptions tested. For cod fishing in Norway, entanglement was also an important contributor, although it was not necessarily the dominant one when other impact categories were included. The results were highly sensitive to the assumed time horizon over which debris remained capable of causing entanglement impacts, which remains a major source of uncertainty.



1.2.3 Additive coverage in LCA
While CFs representing the environmental impacts of plastic emissions have been developed and continue to evolve, most available developments focus on physical impacts and therefore exclude chemical impacts associated with the specific chemical composition of plastic products (Woods et al. 2021; Lavoie et al. 2022; Corella-Puertas et al. 2023; Saadi et al. 2025; Louvet et al. 2026). Plastic products can contain important amounts of chemical additives used to modify or enhance product properties, including plasticizers, flame retardants, pigments, antistatic agents, biocides, and light stabilizers, which can leach out of plastic items (Vincoff et al. 2024; Monclús et al. 2025). This issue has been recognized within the MarILCA framework but is not addressed by the CFs introduced in the previous section. The physical effects on biota pathway characterizes plastic particles through their polymer fraction and does not account for formulation-specific additives. By contrast, chemical effects associated with additives could be represented through ecotoxicity-related modeling, provided that the identity, amount, release, fate, and toxicity of the relevant substances can be specified (Woods et al. 2021; Lavoie et al. 2022; Corella-Puertas et al. 2023). However, as reported by Logan et al. (2024), additive coverage in LCI databases remains highly limited, partly because exact formulations are often unavailable due to industrial confidentiality and competitiveness concerns (Law et al. 2024). Additionally, many additives are currently not covered by USEtox, preventing the derivation of CFs for their ecotoxicity.
Current assessments suggest that most potential impacts on Ecosystem Quality attributable to plastic emissions are associated with the polymer fraction (via physical effects) rather than with additive substances (via ecotoxicity) leaching from plastic items (Lavoie et al., under review). These results indicate that the main contributors to Ecosystem Quality impacts may already be captured by the physical effects on biota CFs. In practice, however, information on the additive composition of plastic items remains too sparse to support precise and systematic impact assessment with the current state of knowledge, and warrants further research and greater transparency on additives in plastics.


1.2.4 Ongoing impact assessment modeling

1.2.4.1 Human toxicity non-cancer (MiP)
MiP emissions to natural environments have the potential to generate impacts on human health through both the inhalation of airborne MiPs and the ingestion of contaminated food and beverages (Lamichhane et al. 2023; Azoulay et al. 2019). Indeed, plants and animals consumed by humans, such as rice, fish, and seafood have been shown to contain non-negligible amounts of MiPs (Dessì et al. 2021; Ribeiro et al. 2020; Anastasopoulou et al. 2018). MiPs have also been detected in multiple human tissues, demonstrating that they can enter the human body, bypass protective barriers, and potentially lead to deleterious health effects (Koelmans et al. 2022; Magana-Arachchi and Wanigatunge 2023).
The impact pathway currently under development considers the distribution of MiPs in the environment after emission, as well as their bioconcentration and bioaccumulation in food. Human exposure, based on region-average diets, is then combined with non-cancer toxicological effects derived from mammalian data, thereby providing a first set of CFs, which are expected to be available in early 2027.


1.2.4.2 Marine biological carbon pump (MiP)
After entering the environment, plastics can be transported to the open ocean, where they can disrupt components of the biological carbon pump (BCP). In fact, MiPs reduce the abundance of phytoplankton and zooplankton (via physical effects), and slow the sinking of zooplankton fecal pellets, increasing remineralization and potentially reducing the fraction of carbon reaching sequestration depth (Cole et al. 2016; Richon et al. 2024; Villarrubia-Gómez et al. 2024). The BCP is a critical ecosystem service responsible for sequestering approximately 20% of annual anthropogenic carbon emissions (DeVries et al. 2023).
LCAs of plastic products often indicate lower carbon footprints compared to alternative materials; however, current life cycle impact assessment methods do not account for climate impacts caused by the effects of MiPs on the BCP. As a result, climate-related trade-offs between plastics and their alternatives may be underestimated. Ongoing work aims to integrate these effects into LCA, allowing for a more accurate comparison of plastics and their alternatives.
This model is currently under development, and the first CFs should be available in 2027.


1.2.4.3 Ingestion of micro- and macroplastics
New developments have also been proposed for combined MiP and MaP ingestion. Indeed, Marhoon et al. (2026) addressed another physical impact pathway associated with plastic emissions: ingestion by marine species, which had already been partially considered in previous work for MiP. The authors developed a global effect factor (EF) to quantify the fraction of marine air-breathing vertebrate species potentially affected by macro- and microplastic ingestion. The model covers marine mammals, seabirds, and sea turtles, and is based on field observations of plastic ingestion prevalence in stranded and bycaught individuals across several ocean basins. Species-specific exposure was estimated using spatially explicit plastic concentration data for floating debris at the ocean surface, combined with species range information. These data were then used to derive dose-response relationships and construct a field-based species sensitivity distribution (SSD).
The resulting EF is expressed in PAF·km³/kg and represents the increase in the fraction of potentially affected species per unit increase in plastic concentration in marine surface water. Marhoon et al. (2026) estimated an HC20EC10 of 51.7 kg/km³, corresponding to an EF of 3.87 × 10⁻³ PAF·km³/kg. This value is approximately three orders of magnitude higher than the EF used for MiP physical effects on biota in Corella-Puertas et al. (2023), which was subsequently applied or further developed in later CF developments such as Saadi et al. (2025) and Louvet et al. (2026). This difference partly reflects the broader scope of the ingestion EF, which covers both macro- and microplastics and is derived from field-based ingestion prevalence data (based on an average plastic concentration per feeding zone), whereas earlier MiP effect modeling is based on laboratory data that accounts for adverse effects (e.g., impacts on mortality, reproduction, and/or growth).
This development is important because it provides a first operational basis for representing plastic ingestion as a specific physical impact pathway in LCIA, including for MaP, for which ingestion impacts had previously not been characterized. However, the EF should be interpreted as an intermediate and generic estimate. It does not quantify observed biological adverse effects following ingestion, but instead assumes that observed ingestion may have led to lethal or sub-lethal physical effects. It is also generic with respect to polymer type, particle shape, and plastic size, and currently focuses only on marine air-breathing vertebrates exposed to floating debris. Marhoon et al. (2026) therefore recommend coupling this EF with appropriate fate modeling before full integration into LCIA, following the broader framework proposed for plastic litter impact assessment.

text:
1.3 Future directions for impact assessment developments

1.3.1 Additional disruptions of the carbon cycle
MiP emissions to natural environments have been shown to interfere with carbon cycling through multiple mechanisms, extending beyond the biological carbon pump disruption. In particular, adverse effects on blue carbon ecosystems or soil biota communities may alter primary production, trophic interactions, microbial respiration processes, and organic carbon turnover, thereby affecting carbon sequestration (Zhu et al. 2025). Such ecological perturbations could translate into measurable shifts in both marine and terrestrial carbon dynamics, although their magnitude and direction remain context-dependent and insufficiently quantified for operational integration into LCIA.
Zhu et al. (2025) further identify additional mechanisms that may appear secondary when considered individually but could cumulatively contribute to broader changes in carbon dynamics. Despite their potential relevance at larger spatial and temporal scales, these pathways are not currently represented in LCIA models. Their integration would require dedicated fate, exposure, and effect modeling frameworks, together with corresponding CFs. Progress in this direction will depend on the availability of sufficiently robust empirical datasets to support quantitative relationships between MiP exposure, ecological responses, and carbon cycle feedbacks.

title: 2  When should plastic impacts be accounted for?
text:
2.1 Client and commissioner intent
Accounting for the impact of plastic litter requires additional attention at both the LCI and LCIA stages. Although some LCIA methods, such as IMPACT World+ v2.1 and GLAM, now include CFs for physical effects on biota, the corresponding elementary flows for plastic litter emissions are generally not available or are not systematically populated in commonly used LCI databases. Consequently, even when practitioners use an LCIA method that includes these CFs, plastic emissions often need to be quantified separately before they can be characterized.
In practice, this means that foreground data may need to be complemented with specific estimates of plastic leakage, while background datasets may not systematically include plastic emissions. Depending on the case study, practitioners may therefore need to perform additional calculations to estimate inventory flows, apply the CFs, or both. This additional work can be valuable, but it may not be necessary or significant for all assessments.
Users should therefore consider the following screening questions before proceeding with a full assessment of contributions from plastic litter emissions. A single yes or no answer does not in itself justify an inclusion or exclusion of plastic emissions in a study. Instead, these questions are meant to stimulate the reasoning of the practitioner regarding the inclusion of plastic emissions.
Questions to guide the decision on including plastic emissions in impact assessment studies.

section: 3.2 Life cycle inventory for the foreground system
text:
3.2 Life cycle inventory for the foreground system
The following steps allow the computation of an inventory of plastic emissions to the environment over the life cycle of the product or service considered. At the inventory stage, details are needed on the emission country and emission compartment, the polymer type, the shape, and the size.

3.2.1 Processes and materials
As a first step in your assessment, the processes in which emissions of plastic pieces or particles can occur must be identified. Here, the focus should be on the foreground system, for reasons mentioned in the previous sections. The processes typically associated with plastic leakage are likely to be similar to the modules identified in the PFN or the PLP. For all types of plastic products, emissions are indeed likely to occur during plastic granulate manufacturing, road transportation with tire abrasion and end-of-life management, including littering. Some processes are associated with specific sectors. For example, the washing of garments and textiles during the use stage is a process in which microfibers are emitted to wastewater. The same reasoning applies to the fishing industry, which can lose fishing gear at sea, and agricultural practices involving mulch films.
For end-of-life processes, it is also important to highlight that leakage could occur via multiple pathways. Littered, uncollected and improperly disposed waste may all end up in natural environments but differ greatly in proportions. Also, waste can be managed suboptimally without necessarily leaking entirely to the environment. This distinction is relevant and justifies the need for a precise identification of processes involved in the targeted systems during the assessment. Some plastic emissions can also originate from waste exports. Indeed, waste mismanagement that occurs once exported waste lands in a country with inefficient waste management infrastructure could also be taken into consideration, if data allow this leakage to be quantified. This is the case for many high-income countries that export a significant fraction of their plastic waste to low- or middle-income countries that rely on poor waste management schemes (Kounina et al. 2024).
The identification of the processes involved in the plastic emissions should allow practitioners to also identify the polymer composition of the emissions, which constitutes relevant information since CFs are available per polymer (e.g., PET, HDPE and PP) or material (e.g., cotton and viscose). This composition of emissions is directly related to the composition of the materials assessed. Therefore, when conducting the environmental assessment of a PET food container, for example, the emissions will consist of PET.

In the example, three processes of the product systems can be identified as potentially emitting plastics to the environment. The distinction between parts of the containers was made because of specific requests from the client. The client was interested in being able to discern whether the potential environmental impacts could be lowered by targeting specific container sub-parts such as lids or secondary packaging. 3.2.2 Geographical location
The geographic location is a key parameter of plastic leakage and impacts. First, the location will affect emission rates of plastic into the environment. In fact, countries and regions with better waste management systems and high-efficiency wastewater treatment plants (WWTP) will lead to smaller emissions of MaP and MiP into the environment, compared to locations with poor waste management and WWTPs. As a result, the same item used in different contexts can lead to different emissions of plastic into the environment.
Second, the location also influences CFs as the fate and effects of MaP and MiP on biota can be regionalized. So far, CFs are therefore available for the following regions: Africa & Middle East, Central Asia, Europe, Latin America, North America, Northern Regions, Oceania, Southeast Asia, and a default World region, following USEtox regionalization (Figure 3.1 shows the available regions). Regional differentiation accounts for parameters such as rainfall rate, water body depth and area, species richness, area fraction, and runoff, all of which influence the environmental fate and ultimate impact of MiP.
Practitioners should therefore identify the country and geographic region in which the processes and activities under study occur, as this determines which regional leakage rate and regional CF values to apply. For instance, road transport activities taking place during distribution stages in North America should be characterized using the North America CF values and emission rates. This same logic applies to manufacturing processes, which may represent another source of MiP emissions and can occur across multiple regions within a single product system. When the location of emission cannot be determined, the World region can be used as the default.







Figure 3.1: Regionalizing environmental compartments: USEtox regions. Source of data: Hajjar and Viveros Santos (2026)





3.2.3 Emission quantity
Following the identification of processes involved in plastic emissions throughout the life cycle of the product system under study, the quantification of these processes must be undertaken. The data used for this purpose may be labeled as emission factors, loss rates, leakage rates, or release rates, and communicates the quantity of plastic (expressed as mass) emitted by a process per unit of activity or per unit of material, for example. Note that mass is currently the designated metric of interest for quantifying plastic emissions. Particle count is also recognized as an important metric in MiP science, particularly for toxicity assessment (Thornton Hampton et al. 2022); however, mass remains the only unit used in the LCA field to date. Accordingly, any data expressed in particle numbers must be converted to mass using information on particle size and density before use in an LCA context. Lavoie et al. (2022) and Besseling et al. (2019) provide worked examples of such conversions.
Various conventions are used throughout the scientific and industrial literature to express quantities of emitted plastics. Emission factors are frequently expressed as percentages or fractions, representing the proportion of a plastic material considered to be emitted to the environment, but may also be expressed as a mass of plastic per unit of process or activity. Some of the variation observed in units and terminology is attributable to differences in what is being quantified. For instance, in the dataset published by the PFN (Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023), some release rates (i.e., RelR) quantify direct environmental emissions, whereas others (i.e., RR) quantify emissions reaching specific environmental compartments following release and subsequent redistribution – whether through natural processes (e.g., transport of MiP from freshwater to oceans via currents) or human interventions (e.g., wastewater treatment). It is therefore essential for practitioners to carefully examine what each data source is expressing and quantifying before use. Some data sources are provided in Section 4 of this guide.

It is important to note that plastic mismanagement and plastic leakage to the environment are not synonymous, and therefore, plastic mismanagement rates cannot directly be used to determine the amount of plastic emitted to the environment. In fact, plastic mismanagement often encompasses open burning and landfilling which are not direct environmental emissions of plastic, but which may lead to environmental leakage of plastic. Data clearly identifying leakage to the environment is needed for this assessment.
A related and critical issue concerns the risk of double-counting fate when estimating quantities of plastic emissions to natural environments. As noted above, emission factors are intended to represent the mass of plastics emitted to the environment at the point of release (initial environmental compartment), while the fate modeling in the CFs accounts for redistribution between compartments. In certain methodological frameworks, however – including the PFN (Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023) and the PLP (Peano et al. 2020) – additional redistribution rates are also provided to account for the subsequent transport of particles between environmental compartments. This creates an inconsistency when these data are combined with CFs for physical effects on biota, since CFs already fully account for the fate of MiP once released to natural compartments. Practitioners drawing on both of these data sources and the physical effects on biota CFs must therefore ensure that only emission values into the initial environmental compartment (i.e., the first environmental compartment that microplastics reach from the technosphere) – and not any further redistribution rates – are carried forward into the impact assessment.

3.2.4 Environmental compartment
Impacts are emission compartment-dependent and are available for the following emission compartments: air, agricultural soil, natural soil, river water, lake water, and sea water (see Table 3.6). In practice, the emission compartment may be straightforward to identify for some processes, but difficult to determine precisely for others.
Precise compartment assignment requires detailed information on where plastic emissions occur and, where relevant, how leaked plastic is transported before reaching the receiving environment. This level of detail is often unavailable to practitioners. Ideally, activity-specific leakage models would provide this information in a similar way as LCI datasets provide elementary flows for a wide range of substances and activities. However, plastic emissions are not yet systematically represented in these data sources. For now, practitioners therefore need to rely on complementary data sources and transparent assumptions.
At the time of writing, the most useful source of information on this matter is provided by the PFN technical modules and accompanying spreadsheets. The release rates in each module include the share of leaked plastic assigned to different receiving compartments. In the PFN data sheets used for this guide, the granularity and completeness of release rates vary by sector (see modules for complete explanation).
For example, in the Macroplastic: Packaging spreadsheet, the “Leaked to Ocean and Waterways” column provides country-specific release rates for a combined marine and freshwater compartment. This helps estimate releases to aquatic environments, but does not distinguish between sea water, river water, and lake water, and therefore does not allow direct selection of the most specific CF. In the same spreadsheet, additional generic release rates are provided for ocean and land, depending on the size of the plastic item emitted and its residual value. Larger items and items with higher residual value are associated with lower release rates. These release rates may not sum to 100%, because the remaining fraction is assumed to be removed, for example through waste picking or municipal cleaning operations. In other modules, such as the textile microfiber module, leakage is distinguished between freshwater and marine environments.
In case no precise environmental compartments are available for the system studied, as a pragmatic default, it is recommended to first apply the generic release rates for “waterways” and land of the PFN to allocate the emitted fraction between continental sea water and continental natural soil, respectively. Alternatively, depending on the country, practitioners may assume that the “Leaked to Ocean and Waterways” fraction is emitted to sea water and that the remaining emitted fraction is released to land, represented here as natural soil. This simplified compartment assignment should be documented, and fractions assumed to be removed or cleaned should not be characterized as emissions.
For MiP emissions from textile production and use, emissions to land should be assigned to agricultural soil since the release pathway occurs via sewage sludge spreading on agricultural fields. Recommendations on compartment assignment are provided in Table 3.6.
For MiP emissions from tire abrasion, it is strongly recommended to use the specific CFs available in Saadi and Boulay (2026), where applicable, as these incorporate a weighting based on the likelihood of emissions reaching different natural compartments at the continental scale. Further parameterization is possible using PFN data to adapt the emission distribution according to watershed size and the share of driving occurring in rural, urban, and highway contexts. Because updates to the PFN methodology and data are expected, these recommendations should be revisited when new versions become available.

3.2.5 Fragmentation
For many of the emitting processes identified previously, the plastic emissions will take the form of MaPs. Yet, CFs for physical effects on biota are only available for micro-sized plastic emissions. Secondary microplastics, which originate from the fragmentation of larger plastics, are nevertheless thought to be the most abundant form of microplastics in comparison with primary microplastics, manufactured as such (Mutuku et al. 2024). This means that MaPs undergo significant fragmentation under forces encountered in the environment. A significant proportion of MaPs that end up in natural environments are going to be fragmented over time, especially over long-term horizons.
On this matter, a few recommendations can be put forward, based on a peer-reviewed degradation and fragmentation model (Tang et al., 2026). A value in percentage (%) is set to consider that only a proportion of MaP emissions are going to be fragmented and should thus be characterized using the CFs for physical effects on biota. Those fragmentation percentages vary depending on material type (i.e., rigid or flexible), and emission compartment (e.g., topsoil, beach or water surface). Since degradation and fragmentation are competing processes on MaPs, the remainder of the MaP that does not fragment will degrade during the same time horizon. The distinction is made here between flexible and rigid plastics, with the hypothesis that a flexible plastic is thinner than a rigid one, leading to the flexible material having a surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) that is larger than that of a rigid polymer, and thus making it more susceptible to fragmentation (Tang et al., 2026). Plastics thicker than 250 µm can be considered rigid (low SA:V), while plastics thinner than 250 µm can be considered flexible (high SA:V). Degradation and fragmentation processes are functions of environmental conditions, which depend on the environmental compartments, namely UV intensity and mechanical forces. CFs expressing damage to biodiversity from MiP emissions span up to six orders of magnitude across the 1–5000 µm size range (Louvet et al. 2026; Saadi and Boulay 2026). Particle size is therefore a critical parameter in LCA, as the choice of size class can significantly influence results. For primary MiP – particles manufactured and released directly at the micro scale – size characterization is generally straightforward, as their dimensions are defined at the point of production and should be known to the practitioner.
The size distribution profile of microplastics generated from fragmentation of macro-sized litter is highly uncertain.
In this context, guidance is provided to practitioners to support that decision. Based on the commonness of microplastic sizes found in the environment and the industry, Corella-Puertas et al. For generic plastic materials (MaPs) (e.g., buoys, plastic packaging, and toys) that have to be characterized as microplastics in order to use the MiP-oriented CFs, the recommended size class is 1000 µm or 5000 µm since large particles will likely dominate the fragmented mass during the early stages of the fragmentation process (Egger et al. 2020; Kaandorp et al. 2021; Ueda et al. 2025). This also matches the recommendations from Corella-Puertas et al. (2023) for fragments of unspecified shape. 3.2.8 Limits of the inventory of plastic emissions
Limits and weaknesses of plastic emission inventories exist and are worth highlighting since they can significantly influence results of the assessment.
Drawing on experience from previous works estimating plastic emissions to natural environments, the most pressing limit of the inventory relates to the fragmentation of MaPs into secondary microplastics, which are then characterized using CFs. Different assumptions have been made in the past (10%, 50% and 100% in Corella-Puertas et al. (2023); UNEP, 2022; 0.5% in Erradhouani et al. (2026); 100% in Louvet et al. (2026); 4%, 12% and 62% in Saadi et al. (2025)), and uncertainty remains on the fragmentation percentage calculated via PlasticFADE (Tang et al., 2026), which reveals the important unknowns associated with this parameter, especially when considering the variety of product types, environmental conditions and polymer chemistry involved, including additives affecting plasticity and fragmentation potential. We therefore recommend always including a sensitivity analysis on the value of this parameter.
A further limitation relates to the focus on the foreground system. Since plastic emissions inventories are not currently assessed in LCI databases, background systems will essentially never include plastic emissions, even though in reality some occur in background packaging, road transport and oceanic freight activities, for example.
Most limits faced during the inventory stage will likely originate from data availability. Some sectors may be unable to find accurate and reliable data on the plastic emissions occurring throughout their supply chain. Because data may come from many sources, methodologies and assumptions may also differ, inducing uncertainty in the assessment. Furthermore, obtaining uncertainty estimates (e.g., confidence intervals) for inventory emission factors is challenging given the current state of knowledge in the field.
Specific limitations are also linked with data sources or methodologies. For example, in low-income countries (LIC) or middle-income countries (MIC), open dumps are the de facto treatment for waste disposal. Yet, some methodologies such as the PFN (Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023) and the PLP (Peano et al. 2020) consider this end-of-life treatment as waste mismanagement and apply a 100% leakage to litter taking this path. There is consensus that open dumps are far from optimal waste management schemes. Yet, using 100% stands in stark contrast to other scientific studies, which instead suggest rates of leakage ranging from 0.04% (Cottom et al. 2024) and 5% (Schwarz et al. 2023) to 25% (OECD 2022).
Similarly, potential plastic emissions resulting from plastic waste exports are also currently not accounted for directly by emission factors provided by the PFN (Plastic Footprint Guidelines 2023). In fact, the share of plastic waste exports is provided, but linking these exports to specific countries and assigning the respective emission factors of waste treated in that country requires additional data and work by the practitioner. It is still possible to proceed to the quantification of emissions resulting from plastic waste exports. To do so, practitioners should rely on waste export shares provided for the country where the end-of-life of their product system is occurring, which is given in the PFN data. Then, identifying the countries of destination for the waste exports would be ideal, but it is also possible to use average waste mismanagement percentages for low and/or middle-income countries provided in the PLP data, and multiply the two values to estimate the resulting emission factors. Then, the release calculation step can be followed normally to identify the emission compartment distribution values.

3.3 Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA)
The previous section introduced the steps needed to obtain life cycle emissions of plastics, in terms of polymer, mass, size, shape and location. Yet, this information alone is insufficient to represent impacts of plastic pollution, as it does not reflect environmental damages associated with the different types of emissions. The following section links the inventory to impact assessment via the use of characterization factors. To generate an impact score, emissions (mass) must be multiplied by the corresponding CFs (impact per mass), for the relevant impact category (e.g., physical effects) and for the LCIA method of interest (IMPACT World+, GLAM, or ReCiPe).
Formally, the impact score is calculated as follows (Equation 3.2):
\[
I = \sum_{i,c} E_{i,c} \times CF_{i,c}
\tag{3.2}\]
where \(I\) is the impact score (e.g., in PDF.m2.yr for IMPACT World+), \(E_{i,c}\) is the mass of MiP emitted by process \(i\) to compartment \(c\) (Equation 3.2), and \(CF_{i,c}\) is the corresponding CF (impact per kg emitted), which depends on the polymer, shape, size, region, and emission compartment of the flow \(E_{i,c}\). Currently, only the physical effects on biota CFs are fully operationalizable, but this guide will be updated as additional impact categories are available for use in LCIA.

3.3.1 Physical effects on biota
The PEBBLE CFs for physical effects on biota express the potential detrimental impacts on ecosystem quality associated with emissions of MiP to natural environments (see Section 1.2.2.1 for more information). They account for both the fate of MiP across environmental compartments and potential effects of MiP on exposed organisms. They are available for two time scales, representing short-term and long-term perspectives offered by different time-horizon perspectives, similar to the Climate change short-term and long-term indicators available in the IMPACT World+ methodology. Using the same approach as Climate change, the short-term physical effects on biota CFs quantify the potential impacts occurring during the 0–100 years time horizon, while long-term CFs quantify those occurring beyond 100 years.
As indicated by the name of the impact category, the current CFs account only for physical effects. This reflects the way the effect factors were developed: they rely on ecotoxicological data from experiments using virgin MiP, in order to isolate the physical effects of plastic particles on organisms, without including potential effects from additives or other chemicals present in plastic product matrices (Lavoie et al. 2022; Corella-Puertas et al. 2022, 2023; Saadi et al. 2025; Louvet et al. 2026; Saadi and Boulay 2026). Chemical substances added to plastic products to modify or enhance their properties, such as additives, are therefore not represented in the physical effects on biota pathway. When relevant and when sufficient inventory and substance-specific data are available, these chemical contributions should instead be considered through existing ecotoxicity impact pathways. Similarly, the fate modeling focuses on the intrinsic properties of the polymer particles, for example degradation and fragmentation behavior, and does not explicitly account for formulation-specific effects such as additional stability induced by additives. Sections 1.2.3 and 3.2.2 discuss the distinction between physical effects on biota and ecotoxicity, and proposes approaches for addressing this issue in practice.
The physical effects considered in this pathway include entanglement, ingestion, and adherence. These mechanisms may lead to adverse outcomes such as mortality, reduced growth, reduced feeding, or reduced reproduction. The CFs are provided for 23 materials, 5 sizes, 3 shapes, 10 environmental compartments and 2 scales (Table 3.19). The CFs can be found in Saadi and Boulay (2026), and the model limitations are discussed in the underlying publication.

The potential environmental impacts of MiP can be assessed separately per ecosystem (i.e., impacts on freshwater, marine, and terrestrial ecosystems), as CFs are provided separately for each. Note that impacts account for MiP transfer between ecosystems, meaning that emissions to terrestrial compartments lead to freshwater and marine impact as well. It is also possible to sum the impacts on all three ecosystems if needed to get a total impact on EQ (and CFs for the total ecosystem impacts are also provided in PEBBLE).

3.3.1.1 Units for various modeling frameworks and LCIA methodologies
Various methodologies are available for practitioners to proceed with the LCIA step of their assessment. These LCIA methodologies combine different models for a number of impact categories and sometimes also imply a series of value choices in their modeling assumptions (e.g., time horizons considered). LCIA methods are considered to be either midpoint or damage oriented, while some methods also cover both (Bulle et al. 2019). The PEBBLE method for the assessment of physical effects on biota impact category provides CFs for both midpoint and damage levels as well and is implemented in IMPACT World+ and GLAM (Bulle et al. 2019; Verones et al. 2026). To facilitate the integration of the CFs for physical effects on biota with diverse LCIA methodologies, they are provided for different LCIA methods in different units, namely IMPACT World+ (in PDF.m2.yr/kg), GLAM (PDF.yr/kg), and ReCiPe (species.yr/kg).

3.3.2 Limits of the impact assessment of plastic emissions
Models are incomplete representations of reality and therefore hold numerous limitations. For the impact assessment of plastic emissions, specifically, many limits can be identified. First, the physical effects on biota CFs are for now only available for MiP-sized plastic particles. Combining this with the uncertainty related to environmental fragmentation processes and the absence of CFs for MaP means that significant fractions of the plastic litter emitted to the environment may not be accounted for in the impact assessment step, specifically for rigid plastics due to their lower fragmentation rates. This results in a systematic underestimation of impacts and creates a mass balance inconsistency: the total mass of plastic recorded in the life cycle inventory is not fully characterized at the impact assessment level, as MaPs are effectively assigned a zero-impact weight by default.
Second, current modeling is limited to the physical effects on biota. This implies that plastic pieces leaking to the environment are assumed to be composed of 100% polymer chains, rather than a mix of polymers and other substances including loose monomers, chemical additives and non-intentionally added substances (NIAS). This omission is explained by the large variety of substances and degrees to which they are present in the different plastic compositions, thus limiting the possibility to provide generic CFs. This might however not be as significant for the impact assessment of plastic litter according to a recent study (Lavoie et al., under review). In that study, authors showed that available additive content for some food-contact plastic items had only a marginal impact on ecosystems (via ecotoxicity impact pathway) compared to the physical effect of the secondary MiP emitted during the fragmentation of the items (Lavoie et al., under review). A dedicated practitioner could include impacts of additives following the method outlined in Lavoie et al. (under review) if additive composition is known or can be extrapolated.
Third, limitations relating to the modeling of the physical effects on biota are reported in the respective papers. They include, but are not limited to (1) the use of a single generic effect factor to represent the physical effect of particles ranging from 0.001 µm to 5000 µm in all aquatic compartments, even though different sizes may induce various levels of toxicity per kg of emissions (Thornton Hampton et al. 2022; Bobori et al. 2022) and (2) the lack of a consistent degradation model for all polymers in all compartments which can distort the residence time of MiP considered in the fate factors (Louvet et al. 2026).
Lastly, it is acknowledged that plastic emissions also lead to detrimental consequences on human health (Human Health area of protection), resource availability and ecosystem services (Resources and Ecosystem services area of protection) (Kumar et al. 2021; Gabisa et al. 2023). Other damages on biodiversity are also possible through interactions with other impact categories such as Climate change, as described in Sections 1.2.4.2 and 1.2.5.1. These impact pathways and characterization models are currently under development within the MarILCA working group and will be added to this guide and its associated tool as they become available.

3.4 Interpretation

3.4.1 Analyzing the results (midpoint, damage)
Multiplying the inventory by the corresponding CFs leads to midpoint and/or endpoint (damage) impacts. These can be added to the results of a conventional LCA study, which considers other impact categories associated with other pollutants emitted over the life cycle of plastic products (e.g., climate change due to greenhouse gas emissions during production). Using LCIA methods such as GLAM, IMPACT World+ or ReCiPe can lead to damage level results, in the same units as those provided for the impact assessment of plastics, such as the PDF.yr impacts for GLAM. The use of the same endpoint indicator allows analyzing trade-offs across impact categories, and the impacts of plastic pollution can therefore be compared to the impacts of other environmental stressors based on the same endpoint unit.
The plastic footprint (at the impact level) could be used as a standalone indicator to compare different plastic alternatives based on their potential impacts on the environment. Yet, it is recommended to include the plastic footprint as part of an LCA that assesses all possible impact categories to avoid regrettable substitutions. For example, the shift from conventional to biodegradable polymers could lower the plastic footprint of a product, yet, it might increase its impacts on climate change if more greenhouse gases are emitted to produce the biodegradable alternative.
It is important to note that key differences in modeling assumptions exist between the physical effects on biota and other impact pathways, even for closely related ones, which may result in impact categories that are not directly comparable. For example, the considerations for what happens when substances reach the sediments or the global scale marine compartment are different in the physical effects on biota model compared to the USEtox model, which addresses ecotoxicity impacts. The current USEtox 2.14 version considers pollutants as being overwhelmingly diluted once they reach this global compartment and therefore models the fate of pollutants reaching the global scale as a removal mechanism from the environment. For MiP, the model was improved and the fate of MiP particles in the global scale is modeled in the same way the continental scale is modeled and thus particles are considered as affecting species at this scale also, even though the locations where concentrations can reach potentially toxic levels are extremely rare (outside of the surface depths near marine gyres, where plastic litter tends to accumulate, in the case of physical effects on biota, for example). Figure 3.2 shows the compartments included and characterized in each method, along with fate factors in each compartment.
Additionally, operationalized LCIA methods (IMPACT World+ and ReCiPe) still rely on ecotoxicity effect factors derived from HC50 (rather than HC20 as for microplastics, following GLAM recommendations). These differences may lead to potentially considerable variations in model outputs. As USEtox 3 becomes available, it is expected that IMPACT World+ will integrate this new recommendation.

Before the PFN (Earth Action, 2023), which has been cited throughout the previous sections as a relevant data source, the PLP (Peano et al., 2020) was the first initiative to support the development of emission factors for activities prone to releasing plastic particles into natural environments. The PFN (Earth Action, 2023) is currently working to publish validated emission factors, although not all sectors have been assessed. At the time of writing, only three of the seven proposed modules have been completed and provide a complete dataset: packaging covering macroplastics from waste mismanagement and littering; textiles, covering macroplastics from end-of-life mismanagement and microplastics from production and use-phase wastewater leakage; and tire abrasion, covering microplastics emissions. National statistics
Data on plastic emissions to the environment are also sometimes compiled by national agencies, with varying levels of granularity, often using material flow analysis (MFA) approaches. For example, Statistics Canada published the Physical Flow Account for Plastic Material in 2025 (Statistics Canada, 2025), which reports plastic flows and stocks from 2012 to 2021. Quantitative data on plastic leaked permanently to the environment are provided alongside other indicators, including total discarded plastic in products, the net stock of plastic in products remaining in use at the end of each year, and plastic products produced for Canadian consumption. These amounts are also reported for a range of product categories, from construction materials and electrical and electronic equipment to packaging, which is further subdivided into bottles, film, non-bottle rigid packaging and other packaging products. This type of data is particularly relevant for estimating emission factors associated with end-of-life management in Canada. Similar national or country-specific data sources may also be available for other contexts. For example, country-specific assessments have been carried out for Switzerland, providing detailed estimates of plastic flows and emissions that can support emission factor development (Kawecki & Nowack, 2019; Jiang & Nowack, 2025).
For information on the impact assessment models, useful data sources include, but are not limited to, the academic literature on the topic, especially the work of the MarILCA team and collaborators. These articles can support understanding of the meaning, scope, development approaches, and values of the CFs developed to date. Many of them also include case studies with transparent documentation of the assumptions and values used throughout the assessment, making them useful sources for inventory-related data as well. title: 6  FAQ
text:
6.1 Scope and applicability
This section addresses common questions that may arise when assessing plastic emissions and their potential environmental impacts in LCA. The questions cover the scope and applicability of the assessment, the estimation of plastic emissions in the life cycle inventory, the selection and use of characterization factors, and the interpretation of results.
The answers provide practical guidance and, where relevant, refer to the corresponding sections and tables of this guide for further detail.

title: 6  FAQ
text:
NoteDo all LCA studies need to include plastic emissions?





No. Whether plastic emissions should be included depends on the goal and scope of the study, the materials involved, the relevance of the flows, and the feasibility of the assessment. Section 2 proposes screening questions to support this decision. No single answer justifies including or excluding plastic emissions; the questions are meant to structure the practitioner’s reasoning.









NoteCan the plastic footprint be used as a standalone indicator?





Yes, the plastic footprint at the impact level can be used as a standalone indicator to compare plastic alternatives based on their potential impacts on the environment. It is nevertheless recommended to include it as part of an LCA covering all relevant impact categories, in order to avoid regrettable substitutions. For example, replacing a conventional polymer by a biodegradable one could lower the plastic footprint while increasing climate change impacts (Section 3.3.1).









NoteAre impacts on human health, on the carbon cycle, or from macroplastic entanglement and ingestion covered?





Not yet, in this edition of the guide. CFs for human toxicity (non-cancer) and for the marine biological carbon pump are under development and expected in 2027 (Section 1.2.4). CFs for macroplastic entanglement (Høiberg et al., 2024) and an effect factor for ingestion (Marhoon et al., 2026) exist but are not fully aligned with the modeling approach used for MiP (Sections 1.2.2.2 and 1.2.4.3).









NotePlastic emission inventory





Why are plastic emissions missing from my LCI database, and what about the background system? Even when an LCIA method includes the CFs, the corresponding elementary flows for plastic litter emissions are generally not available, or not systematically populated, in commonly used LCI databases (Section 2). Plastic emissions must therefore be quantified separately, mainly for the foreground system. Background systems will essentially not include plastic emissions, which is a limitation that should be acknowledged in the interpretation (Section 3.1.8).









NoteWhich data sources can I use to estimate plastic emissions?





The main sources currently available are the Plastic Footprint Network (PFN) technical modules, the Plastic Leak Project (PLP) sectorial guidance, and national statistics or country-specific assessments (Section 4, Tables 4.1 and 4.2). At the time of writing, three of the seven PFN modules are complete: packaging, textiles, and tire abrasion. Practitioners should check what each data source expresses (e.g., direct emissions or emissions after redistribution) before using it (Section 3.1.3).









NoteCan plastic mismanagement rates be used as emission factors?





No. Plastic mismanagement and plastic leakage to the environment are not synonymous. Mismanagement often includes open burning and landfilling, which are not direct emissions of plastic to the environment, although they may lead to leakage. Data that clearly identify leakage to the environment are needed (Section 3.1.3).









NoteHow do I choose the emission compartment when it is not known?





As a pragmatic default, the generic PFN release rates for waterways and land can be used to allocate emissions to continental sea water and continental natural soil, respectively. For microplastic emissions from textiles, emissions to land should be assigned to agricultural soil. Fractions assumed to be removed or cleaned should not be characterized as emissions, and the assumptions made should be documented (Section 3.1.4 and Table 3.5).









NoteThe CFs are only available for microplastics. How should macroplastic emissions be handled?





The fraction of MaP emissions that fragments into MiP is estimated using fragmentation rates that depend on the material type (rigid or flexible) and on the emission compartment (Table 3.7) and is then characterized with the CFs. The remaining fraction is currently not characterized, which leads to an underestimation of impacts. A sensitivity analysis on the fragmentation rate is therefore recommended (Sections 3.1.5, 3.1.8, and 3.2.2).

title: 6  FAQ
text:
6.2 Characterization factors and LCIA






NoteWhat type of effects are accounted for in the physical effects on biota characterization factors?





The CFs represent the physical effects of microplastic (MiP) particles on biota, namely entanglement, ingestion, and adherence, which may lead to mortality or to reduced growth, feeding, or reproduction (Section 3.2.1). They are derived from ecotoxicological experiments using virgin particles and therefore do not include the chemical effects of additives (Sections 1.2.3 and 3.2.2). They are available for freshwater, marine, and terrestrial ecosystems and are expressed under the area of protection Ecosystem Quality.









NoteWhere to find the most up-to-date set of characterization factors?





The PEBBLE CFs (Saadi et al., 2026) are the most up-to-date set of CFs for physical effects on biota. They are implemented in IMPACT World+ and GLAM (Section 3.2.1), and the free online tool that accompanies this guide facilitates the calculations. Future CFs developed by the MarILCA working group will be added to this guide and its tool as they become available (Section 1.2.4).









NoteWhich particle shape and size should I use when they are unknown?





Unspecified shapes are considered spherical (Table 3.9). Default sizes by shape are provided in Table 3.11: 1000 µm for spheres, 10 µm for fibers, and 100 µm for film fragments, with a range of 1000 to 5000 µm for unspecified shapes. For film-like MaP, the thickness of the item can be used to estimate the size of the resulting MiP. Because CFs vary considerably with particle size, this choice should be documented and tested (Sections 3.1.6 and 3.1.7).









NoteIn which units are the CFs provided, and which ones should I use?





The CFs are provided at midpoint and damage levels, in PDF.m2.yr/kg for IMPACT World+, PDF.yr/kg for GLAM, and species.yr/kg for ReCiPe. The units to use are those of the LCIA method applied to the other impact categories of the study, so that results can be combined and compared (Section 3.2.1.1).









NoteWhat is the difference between short-term and long-term CFs, and which ones should I use?





The short-term CFs quantify the potential impacts occurring during the first 100 years, and the long-term CFs those occurring beyond 100 years, similarly to the short-term and long-term Climate change indicators of IMPACT World+ (Section 3.2.1). As for climate change, this choice reflects a value choice regarding the time perspective and should be stated transparently in the goal and scope of the study.









NoteAre the impacts of chemical additives included?





No. The current CFs only account for the physical effects of polymer particles. When the identity, amount, release, fate, and toxicity of additives are known, their impacts can be assessed through existing ecotoxicity impact pathways (Sections 1.2.3 and 3.2.2). Current evidence suggests that most potential impacts on Ecosystem Quality are associated with the polymer fraction rather than with the additives (Lavoie et al., under review).

title: 6  FAQ
text:
6.3 Interpretation






NoteMy results seem incoherent, what should I look for specifically when revising my assessment?





The most frequent sources of inconsistency are the following: (1) units, as emitted masses must be expressed in kg and the CF units must match the LCIA method used (Section 3.2.1.1); (2) emission factors, which must represent emissions at the point of release and not mismanagement rates or redistribution rates, to avoid double-counting fate (Section 3.1.3); (3) the region and emission compartment assigned to each flow (Sections 3.1.2 and 3.1.4); (4) the fragmentation of macroplastics (MaP), as only the fragmenting fraction can be characterized (Section 3.1.5); (5) the particle shape and size, since CFs can vary by up to six orders of magnitude across sizes (Sections 3.1.6 and 3.1.7); and (6) the choice between short-term and long-term CFs (Section 3.2.1).
